scenes.heading: Error Budgets
scenes.narration: An error budget turns reliability into a currency you can spend, making trade-offs between speed and stability explicit.

scenes.heading: What an error budget is
bullets: The allowed unreliability implied by your SLO
100% minus the objective equals the budget
Spent by outages, late data, and bad records
Refilled as the measurement window rolls forward
scenes.narration: The error budget is simply the failure your objective permits: if you target ninety-nine percent, one percent is your budget to spend. Every outage, late load, or batch of bad records draws down that balance. Because objectives are measured over a rolling window, the budget refills as old failures age out.

scenes.heading: How teams use it
scenes.narration: Once the objective is set, you continuously track how fast the budget is burning. While budget remains, teams are free to ship features and take risks. When the budget runs dry, the same policy says stop shipping and spend the next cycle hardening reliability instead.

scenes.heading: The core trade-off
scenes.narration: A healthy budget is permission to move quickly and experiment, because you can absorb the occasional stumble. An exhausted budget flips the incentive, forcing the team to slow down and prioritize fixes. This shared rule replaces endless arguments between shipping fast and staying reliable.

scenes.text: One hundred percent reliability is the wrong target — the error budget lets you spend a controlled amount of failure to move faster.
scenes.narration: Perfect reliability is neither achievable nor desirable, and the error budget gives you a disciplined way to spend a little failure in exchange for speed.
